historical_timeline.summary: Born in the Jorasanko mansion, Calcutta.
His school at Santiniketan begins formally.
Loses consciousness; comatose and near death for a time.
Falls seriously ill at Kalimpong with lower abdominal pain and a severe urinary infection; brought back to Calcutta.
Confined to the house by illness; seeks allopathic, homeopathic, and ayurvedic treatment.

claims.statement: Rabindranath Tagore was born on 7 May 1861 in the Jorasanko mansion in Calcutta, the youngest son of Debendranath Tagore, a leader of the Brahmo Samaj; the name Tagore is the anglicised transliteration of Thakur.

He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913 "because of his profoundly sensitive, fresh and beautiful verse, by which, with consummate skill, he has made his poetic thought, expressed in his own English words, a part of the literature of the West".
He started a school at Santiniketan that began formally on 22 December 1901 with five students, and around it he built Visva-Bharati, an unconventional university.
He was known by the sobriquets Gurudeb, Kobiguru, and Bishwokobi.

His last five years were marked by chronic pain and two long periods of illness: in late 1937 he lost consciousness and remained comatose and near death for a time, and in late 1940 a similar spell followed, from which he never recovered.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The 1937 illness is not further characterized in the sources read.

claims.statement: On 15 September 1940, while visiting Kalimpong, he fell seriously ill with severe pain in his lower abdomen; doctors diagnosed a severe urinary tract infection, and he was brought back, unconscious, to Calcutta.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the synthetic urinary history.

claims.statement: In the last two years of his life illness confined him to the house, with swollen feet, numbness of the fingers, and frequent fevers; women of his family and household nursed him at home.

He sought cure in allopathy, homeopathy, and ayurvedic medicine; physicians including Bidhan Chandra Roy and Nilratan Sarkar supervised his treatment; he is reported to have refused surgery despite repeated insistence from his doctors, to have sought a herbal cure, and to have said that he was more afraid of complicated medical treatment than of death.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the documented preference in the synthetic episode; included with respect.

claims.statement: He was very anxious about the operation and asked several times whether it would hurt; a few days before it he asked for a prayer-poem asking not for rescue from danger but for courage in it.

He was operated on at Jorasanko, on a veranda outside his room made into an operating theatre, on 30 July 1941; one reference work instead says he dictated a poem on 30 July, a day before a scheduled operation.
Doctors reviewing his records for a 2016 exhibition said he had an enlarged prostate that was stopping his urine flow.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective medical reading of his final illness.

claims.statement: Accounts of the operation differ: one says the doctors could not operate on the enlarged prostate and instead performed a bypass to drain the accumulated urine and relieve pain; another says the operation was performed and was successful.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The nature of the operation is reported inconsistently.

claims.statement: Present-day doctors believe that infection after the operation led to septicaemia and his death.
A university vice-chancellor said in 2018 that he was suffering from cancer in his prostate; other accounts describe only an enlarged prostate.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Not adopted; the synthetic episode makes no cancer diagnosis and does not suggest one.

claims.statement: He died on 7 August 1941, aged 80, at the Jorasanko house, after a prolonged period of suffering.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Record the death as a fact without detail.

claims.statement: He suffered the untimely deaths of his wife and three of his children; he took his daughter Renuka to hill stations in the Himalayas for her recovery from tuberculosis.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Evaluation and management of lower urinary tract symptoms with urinary retention in a 79-year-old man, on the AUA benign prostatic hyperplasia guideline (2021, amended 2023), the AUA white paper on nonneurogenic chronic urinary retention, and the CMID benign prostatic hyperplasia monograph: the IPSS, post-void residual, urinalysis and culture, creatinine and kidney ultrasound for obstruction, PSA with shared decision-making about what it means at his age, an indwelling catheter with catheter-associated infection prevention and treatment (IDSA 2009), an alpha-blocker before a trial without catheter, a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor for a large prostate, surgical options (laser enucleation, transurethral resection, and less invasive procedures such as prostatic artery embolization) weighed against frailty, a geriatric assessment (falls with alpha-blockers, delirium risk, cognition) with the AGS Beers Criteria 2023, a goals-of-care conversation, and his own values about surgery and his traditional remedies, recorded in his own terms and respected.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Tagore returns two weeks after an indwelling catheter drained 680 mL from his bladder and tamsulosin 0.4 mg at bedtime was started. referral.pertinent_history: Mr. Tagore is a 79-year-old poet and teacher with months of a weak stream, straining, intermittency, dribbling, frequency, urgency, and nocturia four times, and lately small voids with a sense that his bladder never empties. Five months ago he had a febrile urinary tract infection with lower abdominal pain while staying in the hills and was treated in hospital. IPSS 26 with a quality-of-life score of 5. Bladder scan 640 mL after an attempt to void; a 16 French catheter drained 680 mL without post-obstructive diuresis. Creatinine 1.42 mg/dL (eGFR 50), urea nitrogen 27 mg/dL; urinalysis without pyuria; urine culture sent. Digital rectal examination: smooth, firm, markedly enlarged, without nodules. After discussion he chose to have a PSA, drawn before the catheter, to help estimate prostate size and guide treatment, knowing that screening for prostate cancer is not recommended at his age and that he would not want treatment for a slow-growing cancer: 4.9 ng/mL. He is independent in daily activities but walks slowly and needs help with travel. He takes a herbal preparation from a practitioner of traditional Indian medicine. He fears an operation and wants to hear every gentler choice. Tamsulosin 0.4 mg at bedtime and a bowel regimen start today; a kidney and bladder ultrasound is booked

assessment.assessment: Bladder outlet obstruction from benign prostatic hyperplasia, without a neurological cause or stricture

assessment.display: Benign prostatic hyperplasia with chronic urinary retention
assessment.assessment: An 85 mL gland with a median lobe, benign by examination. PSA density about 0.06 fits benign enlargement; with his age, his goals, and a benign examination, no prostate MRI or biopsy is advised. The retention is chronic and was symptomatic. The raised creatinine has recovered with drainage and there is no hydronephrosis, so it is low risk now that it is drained. The trabeculated bladder suggests long-standing obstruction, and a first trial without catheter may fail

recommendations: Start finasteride 5 mg daily now: with an 85 mL prostate it should shrink the gland by about a quarter over three to six months; double later PSA values for interpretation, with a new baseline at about six months
Continue tamsulosin 0.4 mg at bedtime; trial without catheter at about six weeks, once any infection is treated

Keep the indwelling urethral catheter, changed every four weeks, with closed drainage and no routine antibiotics; intermittent self-catheterization is the better option if he is willing and able, and a suprapubic catheter if long-term drainage is needed

If the trial fails, I would recommend an operation for refractory retention: laser enucleation (HoLEP) is the best choice for this size, under spinal or general anesthesia; transurethral resection or simple prostatectomy are alternatives. Prostatic artery embolization under local anesthesia is a less invasive option with lower and less durable success. Prostatic urethral lift and water vapor therapy are not well suited to this size, a median lobe, and retention
Before any decision, a geriatric assessment of frailty, gait, cognition, and delirium risk, and a frank discussion of his goals

If he declines a procedure after a failed trial, a long-term catheter or a second trial after three to six months of finasteride are reasonable choices; reconsider a procedure for recurrent infection, bleeding, stones, or kidney harm
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Sengupta the same day; Mr. Tagore agrees with starting finasteride and the plan for a trial without catheter, and wants time to think about any procedure
